source.title: Learning curves for deep structured Gaussian feature models

record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically studies generalization curves in deep linear random feature models, a different model and method from the original double-descent studies, and reports how risk changes with width and training-data density.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own learning-curve results for varying width and data density, including an explicit statement that these models do not exhibit multiple descents. Prior-work results mentioned for comparison are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper derives replica-method learning curves for ridgeless deep linear Gaussian random-feature models. Its formulas show test error diverging at the width threshold (αmin=1) and the sample threshold (α0=1, with label noise), then falling again. This bears on whether double descent holds in another model class (V4), on sample-wise non-monotonicity (V3) and on its noise dependence (V6). The models are random-feature models in which only the readout is trained, not trained deep networks, so V1 is not tested. The peak results reduce to prior work in the unstructured case; the new content is that weight structure leaves the phase diagram unchanged.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. In ridgeless deep linear RFMs, weight structure beyond the first layer is generally harmful, while first-layer (input-side) structure, like data structure, can help in the target-averaged noiseless case. Weight structure leaves the phase diagram and its threshold divergences unchanged, and the models show no multiple descents. Weight power-law exponents do not change scaling laws. With the Gibbs estimator at large prior variance, structure can help.
record.recipe_differences: The paper derives asymptotic generalization errors for deep linear Gaussian random feature models using replica methods; it does not reproduce the original empirical deep-network training and measurement procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curves depend on the data-density and hidden-layer-width ratios, label-noise level, covariance spectra, teacher specification, and estimator. The paper also distinguishes ridgeless regression from the Gibbs estimator.

fits_no_version.finding: Anisotropic weight structure beyond the first layer never lowers ridgeless error and does not change the phase diagram or the divergence locations; first-layer structure acts like data structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In deep linear RFMs, weight covariance structure leaves the location of interpolation-threshold divergences unchanged.

record.code_released: Code to reproduce figures is archived as online supplemental material; URL not stated.
record.problems: The main results are asymptotic theoretical predictions derived using a non-rigorous replica method. The studied models are linear Gaussian random feature models with fixed random features, not general representation-learning networks. Numerical experiments are reported for the figures, but the rowed theoretical formulas do not provide uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out.

untested.parts: No trained deep networks; only fixed-feature linear RFMs with a trained readout.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
Whether optimally tuned ridge removes the peak (only ridgeless is analysed; finite λ is left to future work). A variance-based mechanism is not tested.

missing.what: Divergence at the thresholds persists for general structured data and weights (Prop. 3.2, Eq. 23), including power-law spectra (Eq. 31). Section 4 states that weight structure does not alter the phase diagram.
missing.locator: Proposition 3.2, Eq. (23); Section 4 first paragraph; Figure 1(b); Corollary 5.1

missing.what: Numerical experiments (n0=1000, 100 realizations, mean ± SE) matching theory. ε vs 1/α0 for α1/α0 from 0.5 to 2 at η=0 and η=1/2 shows the noisy peak near 1/α0=1 and the width dependence.
Explicit statement that these deep linear models show no multiple descents. It is captured only in row notes, not as its own row.

record.verdict_notes: Width axis (my reading of Eq. 25): error rises monotonically from 1 in the bottlenecked regime and has no classical first descent or U-shape before the peak. The second descent does fall below the small-width error. The double-descent formulas in the unstructured case reproduce prior work (Hastie et al., Rocks & Mehta, Zavatone-Veth et al. 2022). The results are replica-based, non-rigorous and asymptotic. I treated RFMs as a different model class (V4) rather than as V1's deep networks.

versions.untested_parts: The tested systems are deep linear random feature models with fixed random features and a trained readout, not general learned deep networks; no finite-size empirical model-size sweep is reported.
Training time or epochs are not varied.
The data-size result is for the stated asymptotic linear random feature settings, including label noise; it does not establish the effect in other model classes.
The tested class is deep linear Gaussian random feature models with ridgeless regression; broader model classes and nonlinear networks are not tested.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper varies label noise and discusses the number of descents, but does not test a variance-based mechanism or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The paper does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that converts the second descent to a U-shape.

rows.subject: deep linear random feature models (RFMs)
rows.size_stated: nℓ/p → αℓ in the thermodynamic limit
rows.stage_stated: ridgeless regression; only the readout is trained
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes generalization as hidden-layer width ratios vary

conditions.value: L = 1 for Figure 1; paper states the phase picture for deeper models is governed by the narrowest hidden layer

rows.value: Equation (25): for α0, αmin > 1, 1 + Σℓ=1ᴸ [1/(αℓ−1)](1−1/α0); for αmin < 1 and αmin < α0, αmin/(1−αmin); for α0 < 1 and α0 < αmin, 0 when η = 0. The text states the error diverges as αmin approaches 1.
rows.note: This is an asymptotic theoretical width curve, not a sweep of ordinary trained deep networks. The paper also states that these deep linear models do not have multiple descents; that statement concerns additional descents, not the interpolation-threshold double-descent curve.
rows.check: Remove V1: deep linear RFMs with fixed random features are not the trained deep networks V1 names. The bottlenecked-regime value is wrong. Eq. (25) with ψ(z)=1/(z+1) gives (1−αmin/α0)/(1−αmin) at η=0, not αmin/(1−αmin). Error is 1 at αmin→0, diverges as αmin→1, and falls to (1−1/α0) at large width. The second descent is below the small-width error, but there is no first descent.

source_check.correct: At η=0: ε=(1+Σℓ=1ᴸ 1/(αℓ−1))(1−1/α0) when α0,αmin>1; ε=(1−αmin/α0)/(1−αmin) when αmin<1 and αmin<α0; ε=0 when α0<1 and α0<αmin.
source_check.locator_found: Corollary 3.2, Eq. (25), p. 5; Figure 1(a), p. 6; Section 4, p. 7.
source_check.problem: The displayed first branch omits parentheses: (1−1/α0) multiplies both 1 and the sum.
